speaker: Li Lu
text: You do three things: consume less, save more, and, to the extent possible, pay down debt.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is exactly what typical middle-class Chinese families have done over the last five years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Domestic demand has been growing slower and slower, to today roughly zero.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Savings have gone up to about 120 percent of GDP, probably the largest savings deposits anywhere in the world, basically RMB 165 trillion.

speaker: Li Lu
text: People have also been through two or three years of roughly zero price increases or slightly negative ones, more or less in that range.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Therefore, they have a bit of a confidence issue when they look to the future.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is one tier of the economy.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But if you look at the other tier, at the Chinese government’s objectives over the last 10 years and five years, you see a remarkably different picture.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Chinese manufacturing has finally broken through from low- to mid-end, firmly into mid- to high-end.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Every single objective of Made in China 2025 has been hit.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the last five years, solving the bottleneck issues has also made tremendous progress.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Take the example of semiconductors.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It turns out that the U.S.-led technology sanctions have been a godsend for the Chinese semiconductor industry because they have one of the most precious things in a market economy – DEMAND.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Ask any entrepreneur what is most important, and they say the order book.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you have revenue, you get the whole ball rolling.

speaker: Li Lu
text: With more revenue comes profit, comes R&D, comes better improvement, comes more revenue.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That happened to the point that, on mature nodes, both the Chinese equipment side and fabrication side have achieved almost complete self- sufficiency.

speaker: Li Lu
text: On more cutting-edge, advanced nodes, they are getting close to self-sufficiency, with a few key missing ingredients.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you keep this way, on its natural course it will happen.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s just one aspect.

speaker: Li Lu
text: One of the key capabilities of generative AI is producing intelligence at scale on demand.

speaker: Li Lu
text: One of the biggest applications is code generation, and that solves a big problem in some of those bottlenecks, primarily the missing layer of operating code systems.

speaker: Li Lu
text: From PCs to servers to semiconductors to CUDA system of Nvidia, one by one, all of those are now being replaced with the help of AI.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This becomes a great equalizer.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Field after field, over the last 10 years, you’ve seen remarkable progress in migrating the basic contours of manufacturing from low- to mid-end to mid- to high-end.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In some areas—new energy, EVs, storage, batteries, you name it, and it goes on and on, heavy machinery—they dominate.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They have become global leaders.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In areas where they have bottlenecks, they have also begun to migrate and close the gap.

speaker: Li Lu
text: At the same time, it comes with very heavy costs to other industries.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Real estate, for example, on an annual new sales basis, we’re now probably down about 70 percent.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That RMB 10 trillion is also exactly how much has been spent on manufacturing upgrading and technology efficiency, about RMB 10 trillion a year.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you look at the diversion, it is around 2021.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That has been the development model if you look back over the last 50 years of China’s development.

speaker: Li Lu
text: At any given time, roughly every 10 years or so in my mind, you get a new set of objectives and targets, and it comes with heavy costs.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Sometimes in the next 10 years, the objective could become the cost.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the early days of industrial takeoff, the environment, air pollution, and rivers all became costs.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the proceeding next 10 years, they became the objectives, and new environmentally friendly technologies were developed.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The polluters were the cost.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the course of urbanization, real estate developers were the objective, building China into what it is, with home ownership and firm middle-class wealth.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the last five or 10 years, they became the cost.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You begin to suffer quite a bit, but overall you see the progress of the country through those periods.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is why you can compress development over a few hundred years into, say, 40 years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But at any given time, as an investor or entrepreneur — and I’m sure all those people from China would strongly identify — you always want to know whether you are the objective or the cost.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Being the cost of a state objective is no fun!

speaker: Li Lu
text: I’m sure all of you intimately know that or have friends involved in the process.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s how it has developed.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Overall, if you give the score, you would say that, of all those changes, you now have a country of such size and population that has finally embarked on a complete course of modernization.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But because of this two-tier economy and the general loss of confidence, you also have a financial market that has been stagnant for 10 years, going nowhere.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Meanwhile, you have some of the greatest companies, globally competitive, trading at very low prices.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Again, you have the bifurcation you see here.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you’re a rational investor and look at the whole picture, you might take a different perspective.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I would say that in today’s market, you probably find a better opportunity set than you would at different times.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s what you want.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I’m going to take questions in a moment.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: While you get your questions ready, raise your hand.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I want to ask you one last question, very quickly.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: You founded Himalaya Capital in 1997.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I arrived at the University of Chicago about the same time as a young assistant professor.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: The world, at least to me — I don’t know how it looked to you then; we didn’t know each other — was very different, or looked very different from how it looks to me now.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It was a world that was open, transnational, where with travel you could do so many things.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It had, I don’t know how to say it, a generosity of spirit that seems to be a little lacking today.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It looks very different to me now.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: How do you see it going forward, and do you incorporate any of those ideas into the way you think about investing?

speaker: Li Lu
text: It’s a great question, Tano.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The world has changed over the last 30 years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: There’s no question about that.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The world order, or the big questions of how the world governs and operates itself, changes on a slow scale.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It takes decades, sometimes a hundred years, for an order to form and transform.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The current world order was founded through two great world wars, which brought the whole world to the brink of collapse.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Coming out of that, an American-led order emerged.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Through the Cold War and the end of the Cold War, it became one order.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Now it’s transforming once again into something yet to be seen, to emerge into what would emerge out of it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Underneath, there is another order that has been steadily forming for the last few hundred years: the economic order.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It forms when more and more countries and populations join in common trade and transact business with each other.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They form a common market.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That common market was finally formed roughly 30 years ago, with the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Virtually all countries and populations began to join one market economy.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What is interesting about this economic order is that, once a common market is formed, it is very difficult for any single country to withdraw voluntarily.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Out of the market comes efficiency, comes the flywheel of continuous improvement along the lines of technology, efficiency, division of labor, trading of resources, and so on.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Any country that withdraws for an extended period would face a great deal of cost.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the end, once it is formed, it is very difficult to disintegrate.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It lasts much longer.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Look at the trade wars and trade frictions over the preceding hundred years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: No matter what frictions and barriers you erect, people find a way to trade through a third country, along the same principles of comparative advantage.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Take U.S.–China trade.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Of course, that has declined, but if you look at overall U.S. trade with Mexico plus ASEAN, they exactly offset it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Basically, U.S.–China trade remains the same, it just goes through a third-party country.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is roughly true in most other markets as well.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the political order, the U.S., having led the globe for 80 years and shouldered most of the costs of ensuring that the economic common market functions as it sees fit, began to realize that the costs and benefits derived from it were probably a bit out of proportion.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It began to voluntarily withdraw some of those responsibilities, not very successfully so far, leaving a vacuum.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The single biggest change in the political order is the rise of China over the last 30 or 40 years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It has become an enormous economic entity, with a complete set of manufacturing and technological self-sufficiency, and a single largest market that is also open, with unified regulation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is a huge change to both the political and economic orders we are witnessing.

speaker: Li Lu
text: At the same time, our mutual dependency, with one single market, has only increased, not decreased, over that period.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I’ll give you one example.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In generative AI, the one thing everybody needs is chips, semiconductor chips.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Where are those chips being made?

speaker: Li Lu
text: Think about all the countries that produce them.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They have one thing in common.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What do you think that might be?

speaker: Li Lu
text: Sorry, I’m not putting you on the spot.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I’m perfectly on the spot.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Now I have to think about semiconductors when I was thinking that I need to open for questions.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: What do they all have in common?
